prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) isolates a precise mechanism. Credit limits depend on the value of durable assets that also serve as productive inputs. A small shock to productivity or net worth therefore moves asset prices, which tighten credit, which depresses activity and asset prices further. This produces amplification, persistence and spillovers across sectors. The idea became a building block of modern macro-finance and of the financial-friction models used in policy institutions. Its relevance was borne out by the 2007-09 crisis and the macroprudential debates that followed. The attribution is the cleanest of the macro-finance options, because one jointly authored paper and its follow-up on liquidity define the core. Nearly three decades of extension give ample confirmation, so maturity is not a concern. After hearing colleagues, I keep this as my first choice. Several members who ranked it independently (Stromberg, Teorell, Fredriksson, Hassler) also stress the clarity of the mechanism. I treat that as consistent with my reading, not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial thematic overlap with the 2022 prize for research on banks and financial crises. The influential accelerator literature is also adjacent. The contribution is a stylised theory with mixed direct empirical identification of the collateral channel. It rests largely on one seminal paper, so its breadth is narrower than the multi-strand programmes behind B038 or B002. A committee that weights empirical credibility and policy visibility heavily could reasonably prefer those candidates.

responses.point: Friberg ranks Kiyotaki-Moore only eighth. He sees overlap with the 2022 prize and with Bernanke's accelerator work, and he treats Gertler and Gilchrist as a separate contribution.
responses.response: I agree that the Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator is a separate strand, and that is why I exclude it from the citation. I would qualify the overlap point. The 2022 recognition concerned the role of banks in the Great Depression and bank-run and intermediation theory. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns borrower-side collateral constraints and the feedback between asset prices and real activity. The two are adjacent but not redundant. I accept that some residual risk of the committee seeing neighbouring ground remains, and I list it as an uncertainty.

responses.point: Teorell proposes adding Mark Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore, crediting him for the financial-accelerator and macro-financial integration line. He also notes that Gertler's credit is less clean than that of the two originators.
responses.response: I take the point that Gertler is a major contributor, but I would keep the award to two. The citation then rests on one mechanism with a clear origin. Adding Gertler would import the accelerator line, which is partly Bernanke's and partly Gilchrist's, and would leave Gilchrist's exclusion hard to justify. Gertler's credit is also split with the New Keynesian entry (B029). Teorell's own remark that Gertler is the least clean attribution supports the narrower pairing.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B038 second and proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz. He notes that the task framework draws on scholars outside the credited names and that shift-share identification has been criticised.
responses.response: I share the view that B038 is a high-quality alternative, and I rank it second. I would qualify the choice of Katz over Dorn. The China-shock papers that give the empirical core are Autor-Dorn-Hanson, while Katz's contribution is the skill-demand and education-technology strand. I think a coherent citation therefore points to the trio with Dorn. I agree that the credit for the task framework is the weak point, and I would not rest a citation on it.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B002 first. She stresses transparent measurement, large samples and credible quasi-experimental design. She regards the timing as adequate though the programme is still young.
responses.response: I agree that the measurement and design quality is exceptional, and I rank B002 third for that reason. My hesitation is about the object of the prize. The long-run causal verdict on neighbourhood effects is still developing, and credit is spread across a very large team with a three-person cap. Those points do not make it weak. They make me less confident than Dreber that this year is the right time, and the case would be stronger after more long-run follow-up. If the committee prefers it, I would support Chetty, Hendren and Friedman.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees enough separation between Kiyotaki-Moore and the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether adding Gertler (and possibly Gilchrist) would produce a more defensible grouping than the two-person core.
How much weight to give to the mixed empirical identification of the collateral channel compared with the more empirical programmes in B038 and B002.
Whether the maturity of B002 and the Katz-versus-Dorn attribution in B038 will be resolved in discussion.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from the supplied profile. I am a macroeconomist, so I may be more familiar with this literature than with others. I co-author frequently with Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair), though neither is credited on B012. Peter Klenow, a long-time co-author, is credited on B023, which is not in my preferred configuration. I have not adjudicated these ties.
